Abstract
Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a key operation
across high-performance computing, graph analytics, and many
more applications. In these applications, the matrix characteristics,
notably non-zero elements per row, can vary widely and impact
which algorithm performs best. Thus, Graphics Processing Unit
(GPU) SpMV algorithms often rely on costly preprocessing to deter-
mine what per-row algorithm to select to achieve high performance.
In this work we combine SpMV preprocessing and the subsequent
per-row processing on the GPU by leveraging the novel “Work
Graphs” GPU programming model—initially designed for graphics
applications—for dynamic on-device self-scheduling. Work Graphs
allow for fine-grain dataflow execution of individual workgroups
using emerging hardware and firmware support. As soon as pre-
processing has generated sufficient work, workgroups of individual
processing kernels are self-scheduled and executed, interleaved
with those of other kernels. This improves cache locality and elimi-
nates host interaction altogether. Across a suite of 59 sparse matri-
ces, the best of various novel Work Graphs SpMV implementations
outperforms state-of-the-art rocSPARSE “LRB” for a single SpMV
by up to 7.19× (mean: 3.35×, SD: 1.89). Furthermore, it achieves
much more stable performance across various sparsity patterns
than the rocSPARSE CSR-General algorithm, and even beats the
advanced rocSPARSE CSR-Adaptive algorithm for up to 92 consecu-
tive SpMV calculations. In addition, compared to rocSPARSE LRB, it
reduces code complexity by 75%. Its memory footprint for support-
ing data structures is a fixed ∼25 MiB independent of matrix size,
compared to rocSPARSE LRB’s data structures that scale with matrix

Introduction
Over the last decades, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have
evolved from fixed-function graphics hardware accelerators to very
flexible data-parallel processors. GPUs excel at bulk-synchronous
parallel computation, but historically struggle with divergent con-
trol flow and irregular or indirect data access patterns. These limi-
tations have come to the fore in recent years, given the dominance
of GPUs in high-performance computing (HPC) where workloads
are often irregular. One such workload is sparse linear algebra—
particularly, sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV). It is a key
operation across a wide range of computational workloads (pre-
sented in Section 3). However, optimizing SpMV for processing on
GPUs is non-trivial since the number of non-zero values per row
can vary drastically in a sparse matrix.

A key contributor to the difficulties of solving such irregular
problems with GPUs is that, while capabilities and performance
expanded, controlling and programming GPUs did not undergo
a similarly revolutionary progression. Programming models are
traditionally built around the Central Processing Unit (CPU, or
host) submitting fixed sequences of kernels to the GPU (device).
The CPU lacks the low-latency control required to manage GPU
work below kernel-granularity. Moreover, the kernel-centric exe-
cution model precludes the GPU from independently adapting the
execution schedule—such as optimizing for data locality or device
occupancy—based on dynamic behavior observed at runtime. Man-
ual optimizations e.g., kernel fusion [41] are possible, but not always
practical, due to programming complexity and the data-dependent
nature of some algorithms, which precludes static optimization.
In response to these issues, ten years ago Orr et al. had pro-
posed an implementation of a dynamic scheduling programming
model called “Channels” [35]. This relies on the GPU frontend—the
Command Processor (CP) —to execute specialized firmware that
monitors “channels” (i.e., queues) of data items to be processed
by a specific kernel. Once enough data items have accumulated in
such a channel, the CP dispatches workgroups of the corresponding
kernel [35].
More recently, a very similar execution model has been intro-
duced by Microsoft in the form of the “GPU Work Graphs” applica-
tion programming interface (API) for Direct3D 12 [36]. This API
specifies a dataflow-oriented GPU programming model, which we
will simply refer to as “Work Graphs”. In this model, nodes (i.e., ker-
nels) can aggregate individual data items before being dispatched—
akin to the aforementioned “Channels.” Work Graphs is supported
by both AMD and Nvidia, the former having disclosed that the
feature is implemented by extending the capabilities of the GPU’s
Command Processor [34]. This permits fully GPU-driven sched-
uling of fine-grained work at the workgroup or wavefront (warp)
level, based on at-runtime dataflow, addressing many crucial limi-
tations of existing GPU programming and execution models.
In this work, we take advantage of the novel dynamic schedul-
ing capabilities underlying the Work Graphs API on AMD GPUs
to develop a new approach to sparse matrix-vector multiplication
(SpMV), and we evaluate it on real hardware. We achieve perfor-
mance improvements of up to 7.19× versus state-of-the-art GPU
SpMV libraries. In addition, the memory required for Work Graphs
is independent of the processed matrix, which can result in signifi-
cant memory savings for matrices with many rows when compared
to state-of-the-art SpMV libraries. Furthermore, Work Graphs al-
lows us to reduce code complexity. Overall, we demonstrate the
value of novel fine-grained work dispatch, on-device work cre-
ation, and adaptive sub-kernel work scheduling capabilities for
GPU compute codes, and lay the groundwork for future research
in GPU-driven scheduling.
In summary, this paper:
• Highlights the shortcomings of coarse-grained GPU schedul-
ing for problems exhibiting fine-grained data-dependencies
and dynamic shapes, such as SpMV (Section 2).
• Defines and implements novel GPU-driven scheduling ap-
proaches for SpMV based on Work Graphs in an HPC envi-
ronment (Section 4),
• Demonstrates that such dynamic scheduling can signifi-
cantly outperform state-of-the-art libraries for single-iteration
SpMV (Section 6.1) and multi-iteration SpMV (Section 6.2)
on AMD GPUs, and
• Reduces the memory requirement for running SpMV on
GPUs and reduces the code complexity of the implementa-
tion (Section 6.3).

Background: GPU Scheduling
Traditional GPU scheduling is predominantly CPU-driven, relying
on static sequences of commands that dictate the execution flow
on the device. The most important commands are “calls” of device
functions in the form of dispatches. A dispatch encodes that a
device function (a “kernel”) is to be executed with a (usually very
large) number of threads, specified as a three-dimensional grid of
workgroups, each group again consisting of a three-dimensional
grid of individual threads. A dispatch is only finished when all its
threads have terminated. In the default command stream in HIP and
CUDA, a subsequent dispatch cannot start until the prior dispatch
is finished [12]. This programming model implicitly assumes that
the smallest units of work for the GPU are large enough to fully
utilize the highly parallel hardware: i.e., sequences of dispatches
are coarse-grained sequences of tasks, each one easily distributed
regularly across thousands of threads.

Dispatches may execute in parallel if they are submitted to sepa-
rate streams. To occupy the GPU fully, one can seek ways to overlap
smaller dispatches in different streams. However, such dispatches
in separate streams must be data-independent of each other; other-
wise, explicit synchronization between streams must be ensured.
Thus, mapping computational problems to this programming model
and then finding optimal schedules for a set of kernels is non-trivial.
2.1
Task Graphs
Task graph frameworks, such as HIP Graphs [5] or CUDA Graphs [1],
are based on a description of a set of kernels as a computational

graph that expresses the dependencies between these kernels. The
host CPU prerecords a series of kernel dispatches and then sends
the bundle of work to the GPU all at once. The GPU then launches
each kernel in sequence once its upstream kernel-level dependen-
cies have run to completion. This reduces host-side overheads by
requiring the host to only launch a single graph to the device, rather
than needing many explicit kernel launch calls.
However, task graphs rely on the traditional, coarse-grained,
kernel-grid programming model outlined in the previous section. As
such, task graph schedules are static sequences of commands from
the GPU’s point of view. This becomes problematic when dynamic
dependencies exist between algorithmic steps [40]—including SpMV
where rows with different, irregular, non-zero element counts must
be processed by different, similarly irregular, numbers of threads to
fully utilize all hardware resources, as illustrated in Figure 1. The
simplest solution in such cases requires costly roundtrips to the
CPU, which can severely hinder performance. Another option is
to prepare dispatches for all possible combinations of kernels and
use on-device conditional execution, which necessitates worst-case
command counts and (potentially) empty launches that must be
skipped by the GPU’s scheduling mechanisms.
Furthermore, task graphs only capture coarse-grained kernel-
level dependencies, as each node represents a full-grid dispatch of
a certain kernel. This is suboptimal when the underlying problem
in actuality only exhibits workgroup-local or even thread-local data
dependencies. This is the case for SpMV, as mentioned above: each
row can be processed independently from all other rows and should
be processed by specialized kernels depending on the row’s length.
In theory, this independent, irregular per-row-processing can start
as soon as a row’s length is computed. However, a task graph can
only operate at kernel-granularity and thus must first determine the
length for all rows before launching a dispatch for each specialized
row processing kernel, consuming all accumulated rows of that
length (which might be 0, requiring the GPU to skip these empty
launches). Consequently, task graphs’ coarse-grained dependency
model and static CPU-based scheduling preclude exploiting the
true dataflow between individual workgroups on the device.
2.2
Persistent Threads
Some researchers have implemented an approximation of dynamic
scheduling guided by fine-grained dataflow on the GPU manu-
ally [38] with some success [25]—even in the SpMV space [32].
However, such approaches often entail significant implementation
effort and complexity as they rely on the “persistent threads” pro-
gramming model, where a single kernel is dispatched to fully occupy
the GPU and executes all sub-kernels in parallel: Individual threads
or wavefronts typically pull work from global software-managed
queues and then branch to specific sub-kernels for processing the
work. While this allows for very flexible on-device “scheduling”,
this flexibility comes at the price of added complexity, wasted re-
sources1, overhead for queue management, and the necessity of
extensive tuning for different GPUs.

2.3
Dataflow and Dynamic Scheduling
True GPU dataflow scheduling requires the capability for the device
to make intelligent sub-kernel work scheduling decisions based on
data dependencies tracked at a sub-kernel granularity (per work-
group or even wavefront). Attempts to provide programmers with
such explicit true on-device launch control have been made through
APIs such as OpenCL’s enqueue_kernel [2] and CUDA’s dynamic
parallelism [8]. These allow kernels to dynamically call other ker-
nels, but still operate with full-kernel dispatches only, and do not
see wide adoption in practice. Concepts like “adaptive task aggrega-
tion” [20] and the aforementioned “channels” [35] were proposed
as architectural and programmatic abstractions for GPUs, assum-
ing a sufficiently powerful command processor (essentially, a small
programmable scheduling CPU on the GPU) to aggregate many
data elements from a data channel into a GPU dispatch. OpenCL
“pipes” [3] and C++ “futures” [22] are similar in ethos.
Elsewhere in the literature, notions of what comprises “dynamic”,
“data-/dependency-driven”, and “fine-grained” scheduling for GPUs
vary widely—though, to our knowledge, no system (besides Work
Graphs) is available that provides fully autonomous GPU-driven
scheduling at sub-kernel granularity and is available on real hard-
ware. “CUDASTF” [11] introduces abstractions of data access in
kernels, which allow the framework to automatically deduce a task
graph based on the dataflow, and exploit inherent task parallelism
to maximize (multi-) device utilization. While this addresses some
difficulties in programming task graphs explicitly, it remains limited
to kernel-level dependencies and prerecorded static schedules, as
discussed above. Durvasula et al. [14] present another method for ef-
ficient task-parallel scheduling on GPUs without requiring explicit
task graph programming. It deduces data dependencies between
kernels at runtime—however, again, at the coarse-grained kernel-
grid level. Further, its software implementation relies exclusively
on CPU-driven kernel launches; a GPU-driven hardware imple-
mentation is only simulated. The simulated “BlockMaestro” system
by Abdolrashidi et al. [7] analyzes finer-grained (workgroup-level)
dependencies for task graph construction, theoretically allowing
for workgroup-granularity launches. However, it does not imple-
ment explicit dataflow in its programming model, and it explicitly
excludes indirect accesses and kernel-launch-time-unknowns from
its dataflow analysis, whereas the capability to deal with those
efficiently is one of the greatest benefits of Work Graphs. Lastly,
the “T3” system by Pati et al. [37] focuses on asynchronous DMA
data transfers in multi-GPU systems, sharing some principles with
Work Graphs but limiting data-flow-driven operations to inter-GPU
DMA transfers rather than arbitrary on-device work.
2.4
GPU Work Graphs
Microsoft’s GPU Work Graphs API is a renewed and substan-
tially extended incarnation of the fundamental concepts of “chan-
nels” [35], focusing on enabling fine-grained dynamic execution on
GPUs while simultaneously reducing GPU programming complex-
ity [36]. Thus, Work Graphs enables the GPU to process complex
and divergent workloads autonomously without needing commu-
nication with the CPU.
A work graph represents a program that consists of multiple
kernels. Kernels are called nodes and are organized into a graph

kernel-level dependencies to per-workgroup or even per-thread
dependencies—much finer-grained than traditional GPU dataflow

Each thread of any node can produce records for other nodes. The
GPU Work Graphs API limits the output allowed per workgroup
and the maximum depth for a graph2. Also, cycles are not allowed
in a work graph except for bounded self-recursion that counts
towards the graph depth. These limits bound worst-case memory
consumption and enable implementations to ensure deadlock-free
execution.
To construct a work graph, programmers can choose from three
different launch modes to specify the details of the data- and launch-
dependencies of nodes:
Broadcasting launch mode resembles traditional kernel dispatches;
that is, an entire grid of workgroups is launched with all threads
consuming a single shared record3. The dispatch grid size can either
be a fixed constant for the node (“fixed expansion”) or be encoded
in the record (“dynamic expansion”). Note how this mode allows
for on-device expansion: a single thread can create a record to be
consumed by an entire grid of consumer threads.
Coalescing nodes only launch a single, fixed-size workgroup in
which all threads can access a shared array of input records. A
coalescing node specifies a maximum number of records one work-
group can handle. Accordingly, the GPU only launches a workgroup
when the specified number of records have been accumulated. How-
ever, a workgroup may be launched with fewer records if necessary.
This allows programmers to break up divergent control flow into
separate nodes that are launched independently once enough co-
herent input data is accumulated.
Finally, Thread mode declares that a single thread consumes a
single record in isolation. Launching coalescing and thread mode
nodes with waves packed as tightly as possible is up to the GPU
vendor’s implementation of Work Graphs.
2.5
Work Graphs on AMD Hardware
On AMD GPUs, Work Graphs support is enabled by the CP, a
scheduling microcontroller on the GPU. Its behavior is not exposed
through any API, being completely vendor-controlled. When pro-
cessing a work graph, according to AMD documentation, it allocates
a record buffer for each node in the graph, and tracks its usage in a
semaphore [34]. When records become available in such a buffer,
the CP checks whether the output of the corresponding node can
fit into the buffer(s) of its child node(s). If this is the case, the CP
updates the corresponding semaphore(s) accordingly and launches
the node. Otherwise, the CP moves on to other nodes deeper in
the graph. This exploits the fact that leaf nodes (i.e., nodes without
child nodes) do not produce output records, and are thus always
safe to schedule. However, leaf nodes do consume input records
clearing their input buffers (and semaphores), which in turn allows
prior nodes to be launched again if they were previously blocked
from being scheduled. This mechanism allows the CP to “clear”
the graph from the leaf nodes backward to resolve situations that

The fine-grained on-device scheduling enabled through this
mechanism leads to interleaved parallel execution, as illustrated
in Figure 1. The dataflow-oriented execution exploits the GPU’s
hardware more efficiently than traditional pre-recorded kernel dis-
patches through HIP/CUDA streams.
The Work Graphs approach for expressing GPU workloads is fun-
damentally different from the aforementioned HIP/CUDA Graphs
apparatus. HIP/CUDA Graphs defines a static, prerecorded bun-
dle of kernels (i.e., entire grids of workgroups) to be sent to the
GPU, wherein a subsequent kernel is launched once all the kernels
upstream of it have run to completion. No dynamic adaptation is
performed, and only kernel-level task dependencies are considered.
By contrast, Work Graphs encodes fine-grained dependencies—
workgroup-level, wavefront-level, or even thread-level—and takes
advantage of advanced GPU hardware and firmware support to
dynamically dispatch finer-than-kernel-granularity work as actual
data dependencies are resolved. This can have significant perfor-
mance advantages for irregular and dynamic workloads, as the
following sections detail for SpMV.

Background: Sparse Linear Algebra on GPUs
Sparse linear algebra, and, in particular, SpMV, is essential to a
wide swath of computational workloads, ranging from molecular
dynamics to BLAS-based graph analytics to general-sparsity in
AI/ML [9, 21, 23, 26, 27, 43]. Various data formats, such as Coordi-
nate (COO) and Compressed Sparse Row (CSR), have been devised
to compress sparse data by storing only non-zero values, which is
essential to avoid excessive storage and computational overhead
for very large matrices. However, formats such as CSR introduce
substantial irregularity in memory access patterns by requiring
multiple levels of indirection. This makes it difficult to achieve high
performance on data-parallel processors such as GPUs, whose com-
pute cores and memory systems are designed for highly regular
work and memory access patterns. Furthermore, since the number
of non-zero values per row (row length) in a given sparse matrix
can vary widely, applying a single parallel processing method to
the whole problem is often inefficient. For instance, in SpMV, as-
signing one GPU thread to process each matrix row may perform
poorly due to long tail latencies when row lengths vary. Mean-
while, another SpMV implementation that uses a full workgroup to
process each row would suffer from poor device occupancy when
processing shorter rows.
Various methods have been proposed to preprocess input matri-
ces in order to assign specific rows to specific workgroups based
on row length [13, 17], and have been successfully deployed in in-
dustry [6]. With the CSR-Adaptive approach [17], the CPU assigns
rows to GPU workgroups such that each workgroup will either
operate on a set of consecutive short rows (permitting the GPU to
load well-coalesced blocks of data into local scratchpad memory
for processing) or on a single longer row. A later refinement [13]
extended this approach to allow multiple workgroups to operate on
each very long row. This approach leads to very fast SpMV perfor-
mance, but the preprocessing method is not readily parallelizable.

Preprocessing may take as much as two orders of magnitude longer
than a subsequent SpMV computation. Since the current prepro-
cessing is performed on the CPU, overhead is further increased due
to additional host-device data movement. Thus, CSR-Adaptive is
an effective solution only when the preprocessing overhead for a
particular sparse matrix can be amortized across a sufficiently large
number of SpMVs (often on the order of 100s of multiplications
with the same matrix).
Applying techniques such as logarithmic radix binning (LRB) [10,
18] has enabled a similar sparse matrix preprocessing approach to
be parallelized and run directly on the GPU [6]. In this approach,
called LRB-SpMV (see Figure 2 and Listing 1), rows are first sorted
by their length into power-of-two size bins, and a separate kernel is
launched to process each separate bin. This limits row length diver-
gence within a particular bin to at most 2× and permits the entire
algorithm—both preprocessing and SpMV—to run on the GPU, dras-
tically reducing preprocessing time mainly due to parallelization
(typically 20× faster than CSR-Adaptive).
Considering both preprocessing and SpMV together, LRB-SpMV
often provides a faster overall solution than CSR-Adaptive for small
numbers of SpMVs per preprocessed matrix. However, performance
per SpMV is generally lower than CSR-Adaptive, since multiple ker-
nel launches are needed and the LRB preprocessing step is generally
less effective at coalescing memory accesses. Additionally, for large
matrices, LRB preprocessing results are too large to be retained in
cache between the preprocessing and computation steps, forcing ad-
ditional round-trips to main memory to store and then re-load these
data for each bin. Overall, LRB-SpMV is strongly memory-bound,
which limits its performance.

4.1
AnyDSL Compiler Framework
To run a work graph on a compatible AMD GPU, we must use
AMD’s Platform Abstraction Library (PAL) [4]—made available to
us as a vendor-provided build with Work Graphs support included.
The difficulty this poses is that the ROCm stack is incompatible with
the PAL backend. While ROCm is a modifiable, open-source stack,
its architecture is built around the low-level HSA library to interface
with the kernel-level driver and the GPU. Extending or changing
this to replace HSA with PAL (the bottom-level library of AMD’s
graphics drivers) was deemed too complex and time-consuming.
Instead, our manual utilization of AMD’s Work Graphs imple-
mentation is based on AnyDSL4, a framework for programming
high-performance libraries [29, 30]. AnyDSL provides a high-level
programming framework with Rust-like syntax [28], which can tar-
get multiple hardware platforms. Crucially, AnyDSL’s architecture
is backend-agnostic and already includes several backend libraries
to target CPUs as well as GPU compute platforms including CUDA,
OpenCL, and ROCm via LLVM.

To support Work Graphs, we extended AnyDSL’s compiler stack,
adding features to (1) describe a work graph at the language level,
(2) emit kernel binaries for each graph node using the LLVM-based

4.2
SpMV based on Work Graphs
4.2.1
“Vanilla” Work Graphs SpMV. As a baseline (i.e., a “vanilla”
implementation) for our SpMV optimization attempts, we directly
map rocSPARSE’s traditional kernel-based LRB implementation
(see Listing 1) to a work graph. As depicted in Figure 3 and out-
lined in Listing 2, the graph comprises a binning node and multiple
downstream SpMV processing nodes which execute the same core
logic as their kernel counterparts in rocSPARSE LRB.
The binning node is a “dynamic expansion” node that is dis-
patched with a grid having one thread per row of the input matrix.
Each thread computes the length of its assigned row in the matrix
and determines the target bin for the row given by ceil(log2(row
length)), corresponding to one of the downstream SpMV pro-
cessing nodes. Each binning thread thus sends the row ID to the
appropriate processing node in the form of a Work Graphs record.
The processing nodes are split into four separate node arrays,
each assigned a different range of bins. The first array of nodes
handles short rows (bins for rows up to length 16) in “thread” launch
mode. Each thread processes a single row in isolation. Each node
is the equivalent of one bin in rocSPARSE’s LRB implementation;
thus, thread divergence due to different row lengths is at most 2×.
The second node array is of “coalescing” launch mode, and is
designed to handle vector-wave rows (row length 17–256). These
rows can be processed efficiently through a loop of weighted sum
reductions across all threads of a single wave. The number of re-
ductions depends on the exact row-length.
The nodes in the third array handle vector-group rows (length
257–1024). Each node defines its workgroup size according to the
non-zero value count of the corresponding bin. All threads in the
group work together to produce the final SpMV, by first performing
a wave-wide reduction step (like the vector-wave rows) in parallel.
This is followed by a workgroup-wide reduction step using group-
shared memory.
Finally, the fourth array of nodes is of “fixed expansion” launch
mode and handles long rows (rows of length greater than 1024).
Each node in the long-rows array performs the SpMV for a sin-
gle row collaboratively with many workgroups. Each workgroup
performs intra-group reduction steps for a sub-section of the long
row through group-shared memory. Then, a single thread of the
workgroup uses floating-point atomics to add the group’s result to
the final output result. The binning node selects the long-row node
with a dispatch dimension closest to the row’s length5 to minimize
overhead of unused workgroups in the dispatch grid6.
The graph execution is started by letting the CPU send a sin-
gle record to the binning node. This triggers a dispatch of the
binning node, which in turn forwards individual rows to the differ-
ent specialized nodes introduced above. The GPU then continues
scheduling and executing nodes until all rows have been binned
and processed, without any host-managed kernel launches or their
attendant launch overhead. Importantly, the GPU may interleave
execution of different nodes, scheduling workgroups according to
actual at-runtime dataflow.

presented in Figure 3b, that caches each record in a “Binning Cache”

6.1.1
General Performance. Figure 4 shows effective GFLOPS achieved
by all algorithms tested against our benchmark suite in this sce-
nario. As can be seen in Figure 4a, RS General outperforms all other
algorithms on matrices with exclusively short rows (“towards the
left” of the plots, due to the ordering of matrices by longest row
length). However, on matrices with many very long rows, its per-
formance deteriorates drastically (e.g., 30× slower than RS Lrb for
matrix “FullChip”). RS Adaptive performs significantly worse than
RS Lrb on all but a few matrices. This is a manifestation of the
expensive CPU-only preproccessing RS Adaptive relies on (which
is intended to be amortized over the course of many SpMV op-
erations with the same matrix) [13]. Since it is not intended for
the single-iteration use case, we exclude RS Adaptive from further
single-iteration analysis. We also exclude WG Cached from further
single-iteration analysis as its performance is virtually identical
to WG Vanilla and it is intended for the multi-iteration use case
evaluated in Section 6.2.
Thus, for better comparability, Figure 4b shows effective GFLOPS
for the remaining SpMV algorithms only. Most notably, RS Gen-
eral achieves high GFLOPs on most matrices, but its performance
deteriorates drastically when faced with the ten matrices in the
test set that have long to very long rows. The work graph variants
exhibit much more stable and, in most cases, faster performance
than RS Lrb.
The speedups compared to RS Lrb are illustrated in Figure 4c.
RS Lrb is faster than WG Vanilla for only a single matrix (“crankseq_2”,
where WG Vanilla is 14% slower). For the remaining 58 matrices,
WG Vanilla beats the rocSPARSE implementation by up to 4.25×
(average: 2.36×, SD: 1.0).
While faster on average (3.35× compared to RS Lrb, SD: 1.89),
WG Fused is more sensitive to matrix shape than WG Vanilla.
WG Fused reaches speedups of up to 7.19×, but is slower than
RS Lrb on 4 matrices (worst: ‘rail4284’, 47% slower than RS Lrb).
Since WG Fused integrates aspects of RS General, this is unsur-
prising. RS General exhibits speedups of up to 12.98× over RS Lrb.
However, it also inflicts slowdowns of up to 29×. This is not a single
outlier, but rather an intrinsic weakness of RS General triggered by
many long or even a few very long rows in a matrix. This pattern be-
comes obvious for 10 matrices with the longest rows in the test set
(see Figure 4c): RS General slows down by an average of more than
3× compared to RS Lrb while WG Vanilla and WG Fused manage
speedups of 2.24× (SD: 0.65) and 2.28× (SD: 1.0), respectively.
6.1.2
Memory System Utilization. The hardware performance coun-
ters presented in Figure 5 give insight into memory system usage
patterns of the different SpMV algorithms under test. The perfor-
mance counter “MemUnitBusyCycles” allows comparing the stress
each algorithm puts on the entire memory system12 during the
SpMV operation. The traditional LRB algorithm spends up to 10×
more cycles on memory transactions than either Work Graphs vari-
ant for many matrices. This is most likely the case because it has
to materialize the binning information for all rows of the entire
matrix and requires several barriers (which perform cache flushes)
throughout the preprocessing phase.
Albeit the traditional LRB algorithm reaches hitrates between
60–90% in the GPU-global L2 cache13 for most matrices, it cannot
translate these relatively high hit rates into overall SpMV perfor-
mance (as shown in Figure 4). Indeed, WG Vanilla is almost on
par with the traditional LRB for L2 cache hit rates. But the best
performing WG Fused has noticeably lower L2 hit rates. However,
WG Fused has higher L1 hit rates on many and higher L0 hit rates
on almost all matrices than both WG Vanilla and the traditional
LRB. Additionally, the “MemUnitBusyCycles” reveal less overall
memory traffic for WG Fused, and (not shown in the figure) this
translates to less cache traffic across all levels of the hierarchy. Com-
bining this data with the observed best overall SpMV performance
of WG Fused, it appears that the approach of fusing the binning
directly with the SpMV processing wherever sensible (i.e., short
rows) not only eliminates most overhead of manifesting binned
row ids either as records or in buffers. It also seems to enable better
sharing of data in the L0 and L1 caches, which is more likely to be
matrix and vector data because of the aforementioned decreased
record memory traffic. Thus, overall the reduced memory overhead
and the better caching in local caches enabled by Work Graphs
correlates with performance in the algorithms examined here.
6.2
Multi-Iteration SpMV
A “Multi-Iteration SpMV” multiplies the same (constant) sparse ma-
trix with a number of different vectors. This is a common scenario
in real-world applications, for example, for iterative solvers [9, 21].
In these cases, SpMV algorithms can amortize one-time preprocess-
ing costs. Figure 6a shows this amortization by plotting the average
absolute runtime across all matrices for different multiplication
counts. RS General performs no preprocessing and thus exhibits a
linear runtime growth with each further multiplication. By contrast,
RS Lrb, and especially RS Adaptive start with a high penalty on
small iteration counts. But then they can amortize their preprocess-
ing with growing iteration counts. RS Adaptive’s multiplication is
much faster, but this only comes into play after ∼40 matrix-vector
multiplications when compared to RS Lrb on the average runtime
per matrix across the entire test set.
Our naïve WG Vanilla executes the binning kernel on the entire
matrix on every run, essentially performing the preprocessing step
for every matrix-vector multiplication. Thus, the preprocessing
is not amortized and runtime scales linearly with the number of
iterations. Despite this, it outperforms RS Lrb up to ∼10 matrix-
vector multiplication iterations and RS Adaptive up to ∼32 iterations.

6.3
Secondary Metrics
Beside raw speed, we compare the different SpMV algorithms with
regards to their memory overhead and overall development com-
plexity. While these secondary metrics do not change performance
evaluation, they can be of great importance when factors such as
maximum problem size, deployment cost, and development time
must be considered.
Memory Overhead: All algorithms under test, except for RS Gen-
eral, build up supporting data structures to deal with the divergent
row lengths in a sparse matrix. These data structures consume
memory on the GPU.
As shown in Figure 7, RS Adaptive’s overhead is almost negli-
gible. While it scales with matrix row count, the largest matrix
in the test set (“kmer_U1a”) only requires 1.6 MiB of supporting
data structures. Contrastingly, RS Lrb’s memory requirements scale
much more drastically with the number of rows of the input matrix.
For very large matrices, this may become prohibitive (“kmer_U1a”:
529 MiB), or reduce the maximum problem size per device. A driver
that supports Work Graphs does not need to supply memory for the
worst-case (i.e., the entire problem), since no global synchronization
points are needed in the data flow-oriented model. Thus, WG Vanilla
requires a constant 41.3 MiB (i.e., less than 10% of RS Lrb’s require-
ment for “kmer_U1a”) and WG Fused even less with 24.8 MiB—both
independent of matrix dimensions. And even WG Cached that must
allocate additional memory to store the binning information for all
rows, scales less aggressively with matrix row count than RS Lrb
does (∼56% of RS Lrb’s requirement for “kmer_U1a”).

7
Conclusion
In this paper, we implemented multiple exclusively GPU-driven
SpMV algorithms that exploit novel dynamic scheduling capabil-
ities introduced to recent GPU hardware generations to support
the GPU Work Graphs programming model. In benchmarks with a
set of 59 sparse matrices, we observed significant performance im-
provements of dynamically scheduled implementations compared
to traditional static kernel schedules. For a single multiplication,
that is, single-iteration SpMV, our direct translation of rocSPARSE’s
LRB algorithm into work graphs (WG Vanilla) outperforms the
production-level RS Lrb implementation on all but a single ma-
trix, reaching up to 4.25× speedup (mean: 2.36×, SD: 1.0). Our
WG Cached work graph extends WG Vanilla with caching tech-
niques to amortize preprocessing, outperforming RS Lrb for any
number of consecutive SpMVs and even besting the multi-iteration
optimized RS Adaptive for up to 40 iterations. A third implementa-
tion, which combines zero-overhead processing of short rows with
separate kernels for longer rows (WG Fused), achieves even higher
performance: single-iteration speedups of up to 7.19× compared to
RS Lrb (mean: 3.35×, SD: 1.89) combined with multi-iteration perfor-
mance that clearly beats RS Lrb and even outperforms RS Adaptive
up to 90+ iterations.

Our Work Graphs-based SpMV implementations achieve such
speedups by performing preprocessing and multiplication entirely
on the GPU without requiring CPU interaction. Additionally, the
ability to let the GPU self-schedule at fine-grained sub-grid/work-
group granularity according to at-runtime dataflow allows for com-
bination of different processing paradigms that otherwise can not
be easily combined. Furthermore, overlapping occupancy of bin-
ning and processing kernels leads to less overall memory traffic and
better utilization of local caches. Finally, Work Graphs require only
a fixed-size memory allocation of tens of megabytes independent
of matrix size and development is simplified. Overall, our work on
SpMV presented in this paper demonstrates the potential value of
dynamic fine-grained on-device scheduling capabilities, such as
Work Graphs, for the HPC space.

Abstract: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a key operation across high-performance computing, graph analytics, and many more applications. In these applications, the matrix characteristics, notably non-zero elements per row, can vary widely and impact which algorithm performs best. Thus, Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) SpMV algorithms often rely on costly preprocessing to deter- mine what per-row algorithm to select to achieve high performance. In this work we combine SpMV preprocessing and the subsequent per-row processing on the GPU by leveraging the novel “Work Graphs” GPU programming model—initially designed for graphics applications—for dynamic on-device self-scheduling. Work Graphs allow for fine-grain dataflow execution of individual workgroups using emerging hardware and firmware support. As soon as pre- processing has generated sufficient work, workgroups of individual processing kernels are self-scheduled and executed, interleaved with those of other kernels. This improves cache locality and elimi- nates host interaction altogether. Across a suite of 59 sparse matri- ces, the best of various novel Work Graphs SpMV implementations outperforms state-of-the-art rocSPARSE “LRB” for a single SpMV by up to 7.19× (mean: 3.35×, SD: 1.89). Furthermore, it achieves much more stable performance across various sparsity patterns than the rocSPARSE CSR-General algorithm, and even beats the advanced rocSPARSE CSR-Adaptive algorithm for up to 92 consecu- tive SpMV calculations. In addition, compared to rocSPARSE LRB, it reduces code complexity by 75%.
